title: Caching and rendering strategy
headline: The caching code is sound, not bloated: 85 cached reads in 49 files, 82 tagged, tags per store, and Kaizena Flow's own site and docs truly static. What is left is rendering that runs per request for little, and it grows with shoppers and stores, not with any unused feature: every store page view runs a render function to place two cart badges and a country hint (97,919 of the demo home's 138,523 bytes); one Add to cart redraws the whole page and re-fetches 15 links (193 KB, measured); Bing, Google's shop and ads crawlers and every link preview get a full render even of the 508 static pages; and links prefetch pages nobody opens (11 to 50 requests a store page, 23 to 46 an admin screen). 16 findings stand (13 from the verified report, 3 added by this pass), 1 was refuted. Do first: the two prefetch cuts, the AI tag, the page-list split and a build check that holds what is static (nothing holds it today); the structural ones (cart count in the browser, deploys that skip superseded pushes, crawlers served from the cache) are cheapest before opening.

clean: Tag discipline: 82 of 85 cached reads carry a tag, almost all per store (store:, pages:, catalog:, terms:, fields:, cookies:, chat:, experiments:, recommend:, campaigns:). The global catalog tag is refreshed only by VAT changes (src/server/vat-admin.ts). That one product save refreshes the whole store's catalogue is already step 3.10 (FF3, Open) of docs/audits/code-review-2026-11.md, so it is not repeated as a finding. A page publish likewise refreshes the whole store's pages (34 refresh sites of pagesTag): the same shape, bounded by one store, and CA-3's per-page read is the first step toward a per-page tag.

Kaizena Flow's own site and the docs are truly static for people: /, /blog, /sign-up and 462 docs routes are compute static in the manifest and answer s-maxage=3600 with stale-while-revalidate (re-measured with curl: / and /docs are cache HITs). Crawlers on Next's list are the exception (CA-15).

The store layout awaits params above any Suspense (src/app/s/[store]/[market]/layout.tsx:105). Next's ISR guide (incremental-static-regeneration-cache-components.md) says this is what creates a kept page per address while Partial Prefetching is off. Correct for the current setting.

refreshTag() (src/server/refresh.ts:10-16) uses updateTag in an action and falls back to revalidateTag(tag, 'max') elsewhere, as Next's docs describe. The dispatcher refreshes page, theme and catalogue tags only for the stores whose schedules, themes or alt texts changed (src/app/api/cron/cart-reminders/route.ts:262-278).

The proxy does not read the database on every request: a store's facts and the house-store switch are remembered 10 s per instance (src/server/redirect-resolve.ts:203-211, src/server/house-switch.ts:30-41). It does run for every matched request, 13 to 44 per store page load today, most of them prefetches (metric above), so CA-4 and SC-1 cut its runs too. On Kaizena Flow's own host it reads the switch before it looks at the path, also for docs pages that never need it (src/proxy.ts:67-70); a three-line reorder, worth doing when the proxy is next touched.

Arguments of cached functions are ids, slugs and the small Market object. The longest cache key on the demo home is 352 characters (re-measured). No whole Store object is passed into a cached function.
Stock, the tiles' facts (/api/shop/tiles), the wishlist and recommendations answer no-store by written rule (D172, D557). Right: they are per visitor or change by the minute.

HTTP caching is well set where it was thought about: product feeds (s-maxage=900), font files (one year, immutable), the fonts catalogue, the site's sitemap and llms.txt (one hour), share pictures (a day in browsers and at the CDN, a week stale: src/lib/share-card.tsx:29), the storefront API's cacheable reads (public, max-age=60: src/server/storefront-route.ts:23).

Public pages keep their metadata static: 386 of 388 prerendered public pages hold <title> before </head> in the static file, and no generateMetadata outside the admin takes searchParams (68 checked by rg). This is what makes CA-15's change safe.
commerce.search_cache keeps AI search answers in the database for 30 days, the right tool for a cache that must outlive an instance and a deploy.
No link uses prefetch={true}, so switching Partial Prefetching on later has no legacy full prefetches to migrate.
Demo store pages are prerendered per market with their product, category and page addresses. They cost build time only (1,426 pages in 28.9 s).

Four small per-instance memos exist (src/server/limits.ts:26, redirect-live.ts:187, experiments.ts:63, holding.ts:19). A duplicate helper, but tiny; CA-9 should reuse remembered() rather than add a fifth.

listGridProducts() keyed by an id list (the auditor's CA-14, refuted): its main callers ask for the same list for every shopper, so the entries are reused inside a warm instance. No cost was measured.

refuted.title: Cache entries keyed by lists of ids are almost never asked for twice
refuted.why: Not supported: the commonest callers (an unfiltered listing's page, a product's related products, a popular search) pass lists that are the same for all shoppers, one caller is itself cached, no hit rate was measured, and the proposed uncached read would add a database read to views a warm instance answers from memory today.

findings.title: Every store page view runs a render function, to place two cart badges and a country hint
findings.evidence: Re-measured in this pass. The prerender manifest marks 148 of the 149 prerendered store routes compute 'resuming' (a function on every view); / is 'static'. Demo home: the shell .next/server/app/s/demo/no.html is 40,604 bytes with 0 flight pushes and three unresolved holes: B:0 after the wishlist link in the header, B:2 before the cart link in the phone bar, B:1 after the footer. The local production server answers 138,523 bytes with Cache-Control private, no-cache, no-store; / answers from the cache (HIT, s-maxage=3600). So 97,919 bytes per view come from the function. Counted in all 147 demo shells: 33 routes have exactly these three holes, listings and search have a fourth (searchParams, rule D78), product pages a fourth or fifth (stock). The three are CartLink twice (cart-link.tsx:26 reads the cart cookie through getCartCount, cart.ts:544) and CountryHintSection (headers(), drawn for a store with more than one country, layout.tsx:226). A static page keeps its page data in the file: index.html is 39,845 bytes with a 991-byte .meta, where the demo home keeps a 19,751-byte .meta of resume data. After load every store page also calls /wishlist/saved (15 bytes, private no-store): a second function run. The three httpOnly cookies that make a visitor 'someone' are set in exactly three places: cart.ts:717, wishlists.ts:44, customers.ts:416.
findings.cost: Per view of a store page: one render function run that redraws the page's server components from the resume data and streams 97,919 bytes after the shell (demo home), plus one function run for the wishlist call. The platform is not open, so today crawlers and testing pay it; it grows one for one with shopper page views.
findings.who_pays: The server per request; the shopper's browser, which waits for the stream before the page wakes up.

findings.title: Cached reads and built pages live in one instance and one deploy; each deploy empties them for every store
findings.evidence: Next's guide, read in this pass: a 'use cache' result stays 'in a per-instance, in-memory store that is ephemeral on serverless', and 'all of these stores are scoped to a single deployment', remote ones included, because the cache key holds the build id (08-caching.md:596-602; use-cache-remote.md:96-104). Measured: all 25 cache keys in the demo home's resume data end with the id in .next/BUILD_ID. src has no 'use cache: remote' and no unstable_cache. Only the template store is built ahead (prerenderedShops(), shop.ts:94-102). 115 store route patterns have no fallback and compute 'blocking', so the first visit to each page of every other store after each deploy waits for a full render: 25 cached reads on the demo home. ci.yml gives every push to main that is not words only its own run, and the run asks Vercel's deploy hook to build 'the head of main at the moment it is called, not this commit' (ci.yml:306-309, D530); so pushes close together each ask for a build of the same or nearly the same head, and an earlier run can deploy a later commit whose quick gate has not finished. The verified report counted 115 commits in two days, 80 of them deployable. Production, 78 days, not open: reads cached for hours still ran 79,778 times (published pages), 70,257 (cookie scans), 53,887 (platform settings), 42,211 (font css): jobs, crawlers, builds and testing on cold instances.
findings.cost: After each deploy: the first visit to any page of any store but the demo is a blocking render with 25 or more database reads (count from the demo home; time not measured), and every instance's cached reads start empty. Each deploy also rebuilds 772 prerendered routes (1,426 pages; 263 s here with the type check). Today's cold runs measure an idle platform, not load.
findings.who_pays: Shoppers of real stores (first view after a deploy), the database, the build.
fix_steps: 1. The owner's choice, for when stores are open: keep one deploy per push (today), or let a run skip its deploy when a newer commit is already on main. The steps below assume the second.

2. .github/workflows/ci.yml, job pending (no migration): the step 'Is a migration pending at the head of main by now?' (line 310) already fetches the head. Add a step after it that compares git rev-parse FETCH_HEAD with GITHUB_SHA; when they differ, set superseded=true and skip the deploy-hook step (line 314) and the wait. The newer push's own run deploys the head after its own gate. Do not skip in the release job: a run that applied a migration deploys, as now.
3. scripts/await-deploy.mjs already accepts a later deployment that includes the commit; a skipped run prints that the head's run deploys it, and ends green.

4. Do not move reads to 'use cache: remote' or unstable_cache now. Remote entries do not survive a deploy and add a network lookup per read (Next's table: persists across deploys, No). unstable_cache does persist across deploys (use-cache.md:256-258) but hands values written by old code to new code, which at this deploy pace risks an old-shaped Store meeting a new build. Revisit after opening with a measured hit rate for loadStore (stores.ts:216) and the platform's loadSettings.

5. Write what 'cached' means beside the Catalogue reads rule in docs/rules/storefront.md:112 and in docs/performance.md: a 'use cache' result lives in one instance's memory and one deployment; a built page lives until the next deployment; only the template store is built ahead, so the first view of any other store's page after a deploy is a full render. New code must not lean on a cached read being warm.
6. After opening, count blocking first views per deploy in Vercel's logs and decide then between building the busiest stores ahead (generateStaticParams) and CA-7's shells.

findings.title: Bing, Google's shop and ads crawlers and every link preview get a full render of every page, static ones included
findings.evidence: Found and measured in this pass. With Cache Components, Next skips the prerendered page for user agents on its 'HTML-limited bots' list and renders the page per request (streaming.md:681-685: such bots 'skip the prerendered shell and render the page dynamically so metadata can be placed in the head'). The build writes the rule into every app page's entry in .next/prerender-manifest.json (experimentalBypassFor, a user-agent matcher; build/index.js:2046-2075: 'For PPR routes, bypass the shell … and produce a dynamic render'), static pages included: /docs has it. Measured on the local production server: with a browser's user agent / and /docs answer x-nextjs-cache HIT, s-maxage=3600; with Bingbot's they answer Cache-Control private, no-cache, no-store and no HIT. The default list (html-bots.js:15), tested with node against 16 user agents: it matches Bingbot, Storebot-Google (Google's shopping crawler), AdsBot-Google, Google-InspectionTool, facebookexternalhit, facebookcatalog (Meta's catalogue crawler), Applebot, Yandex and Slackbot; it does not match Googlebot, GPTBot or ClaudeBot, which get what a browser gets. next.config.ts does not set htmlLimitedBots. The reason for the bypass does not hold here: 386 of 388 prerendered public pages already have <title> before </head> in the static file (the two others are the docs search pages), and none of the 68 generateMetadata functions outside the admin takes searchParams. A render made for a bot is not kept, so a crawler's visit does not warm the page for the next person.
findings.cost: One full page render per crawler request, on a mostly cold instance, with every cached read the page uses (25 on the demo home) asked of the database; also for the 508 pages a person gets from the cache. Volume in production is not known (not queried in this review). It grows with stores, products and feeds: the shopping and catalogue crawlers visit every product a feed lists. Before opening, crawlers are a large share of the little traffic there is, which fits production's counts of 'cached' reads that still ran.
findings.who_pays: The server per crawler request; the database.
fix_steps: 1. Measure first, outside this review: in Vercel's logs, count page-route function runs over 7 days whose user agent matches Next's default list (html-bots.js:15) against all page-route runs. If the share is small after opening, stop here.

2. Hold the property that makes the bypass unnecessary: CA-16's script checks that every prerendered public page has <title> and og:title before </head> in its static file (386 of 388 today; list the docs search pages as the exception).

3. next.config.ts, beside cacheComponents: add htmlLimitedBots with a pattern that keeps only the link-preview fetchers, which never run scripts and come once per shared link: /facebookexternalhit|Twitterbot|LinkedInBot|Slackbot|Discordbot|WhatsApp|SkypeUriPreview|redditbot|quora link preview|vkShare|tumblr|bitlybot/i. The config replaces Next's list (htmlLimitedBots.md), so Bing, Yandex, Baidu, Applebot, DuckDuckBot, every *-Google and Google-* fetcher and facebookcatalog then get what Googlebot already gets: the static file, or the shell and the stream. A comment says why.
4. Check after a build: experimentalBypassFor in .next/prerender-manifest.json carries the new pattern, and curl -A 'bingbot' on pnpm start gets x-nextjs-cache: HIT for / and /docs.

5. New e2e test (request API, no scripts, Bingbot's user agent): the demo home, a product page, a category page and a blog article each hold title, description, canonical, og:title, the product's name and price, and the product's JSON-LD somewhere in the HTML.
